# Tidewater crew handbook

This handbook applies to everyone who works on board a Tidewater vessel:
masters, officers, engineers, deckhands and the catering team. It is
reviewed every January by the marine superintendent, and changes are
briefed to every crew at the first drill of the year.

## Watch system

The route vessels run a two-watch system during the summer timetable and a
single long day during the winter timetable. In summer, the early watch
takes the first sailing from Harlow and hands over at the Harlow berth after
the fourth round trip; the late watch takes the rest of the day and brings
the vessel back to the Harlow berth for the night. In winter, one crew works
the whole shorter timetable.

Handover always takes place alongside at Harlow, never at Pellin Island or
Dunmere, and the incoming master and chief engineer must each walk the
vessel with their outgoing counterpart before signing the handover sheet.
A handover that is not signed by both masters means the outgoing master
remains in command.

## Rest hours

Rest hours are recorded in the rest-hours register on board and checked
weekly by the marine superintendent. The legal minimum applies to everyone,
but Tidewater's own rules are stricter for the roles that do the most
physical work or keep a navigational watch, and the stricter rule always
wins.

Every crew member must have at least 77 hours of rest in any seven-day
period. Masters and officers of the watch must have at least 12 hours of
rest between the end of one duty and the start of the next. Engineers who
were called out during the night must have 8 hours of uninterrupted rest
before they return to duty, even if this delays the first sailing.
Deckhands, who handle the mooring lines and the vehicle deck, must have at
least 13 hours of rest between shifts, and a deckhand may not work more than
five consecutive days without two full days off.

## Minimum crew

The minimum crew is the smallest crew with which a vessel may sail. It is
set by the safe manning document and by Tidewater's own rules, which add
crew for night sailings and for sailings with vehicles on board.

MV Osprey sails with a minimum of 4 crew by day and 5 by night. MV Kestrel
sails with a minimum of 5 crew by day. At night, MV Kestrel needs a minimum
of 7 crew: the master, the chief officer, the chief engineer, a second
engineer and three deckhands. On every night sailing, the person holding the
night-navigation endorsement must be the chief officer; if the chief officer
does not hold it, the sailing is cancelled rather than crewed with someone
else. A sailing that cannot meet its minimum crew is cancelled, and
passengers are offered the weather-cancellation terms.

## Drills

Every crew holds a fire drill and an abandon-ship drill every week, and a
man-overboard drill every month. The man-overboard drill is timed from the
moment the alarm is raised to the moment the dummy is recovered on deck;
the target is 4 minutes. Every drill is logged with its time and the names
of the crew who took part.

In 2025 the fleet held 36 man-overboard drills. Drill Q1-02 (MV Kestrel, off
Harlow) recovered the dummy in 3 minutes 10 seconds, and drill Q2-04 (MV
Osprey, off Dunmere) met the target with 50 seconds to spare. Only one drill
missed the target: drill Q3-11, held by MV Kestrel off Pellin Island in a
rising swell, recovered the dummy 40 seconds late because the rescue boat's
davit jammed. The davit was replaced the following week, and the drill was
repeated successfully.

## Uniform and personal equipment

Deck crew wear the Tidewater navy uniform with high-visibility vests on the
vehicle deck and during mooring. Safety boots and a helmet are required on
the vehicle deck at all times. Engineers wear flame-retardant overalls in
the engine room and hearing protection whenever an engine is running.
Catering staff wear the white Tidewater tunic and are issued non-slip shoes.

## Training

New crew complete a two-day familiarisation on each vessel they will work
on before they are counted in the minimum crew. Every crew member repeats
the basic sea-survival course every five years. Masters and chief officers
complete a bridge-resource-management refresher every three years, and the
night-navigation endorsement is renewed every two years with a night sea
trial on the Dunmere route.
